title: Chapter 165 – Duan's Sword
html:
[The Hall of the Sixth Door – Lin Jian]

The shadow in the corridor, it turns out, was afraid of the boy.

Jian learns this on the morning of the twelfth day, from Zhen Li himself, who tells it with the dry precision of a child reporting on the weather. He remembers the shadow only dimly now. It stood at the end of the dark passage beyond the seventh lamp, tall and thin and wrong, with no face and too many joints. He walked toward it with the brass lamp raised. At ten paces it began to shrink. At five it was a smudge on the floor. At two it was gone, with a sound like a wet cloth drawn through a crack.

"It went down the drain," Zhen Li says. He is sitting on the Annex floor with his knees drawn up, polishing the lamp's spout with the hem of his smock. "There's a drain at the end of the passage. A round one, with bars. It slid between the bars."

"A scout," says Jian.

"I think so. It was looking." He frowns, trying to hold the memory. "I don't remember what it looked like. But I remember that it was glad to go."

Jian sits down on the cot opposite. His legs are better today. He has walked the length of the Annex corridor twice, once with Bell and once alone, and nobody has shouted at him for it. He feels, for the first time in a long while, nearly like a man.

"How many lamps now?" he asks.

"A hundred and nineteen." Zhen Li looks at the brass in his hands. "I think I can do more. But Nurse says I have to eat first."

"Nurse is right."

"She always is." A flicker of a smile. "I wish I could remember why that's funny."

* * *

Mei has recovered to fifty-eight percent.

Ethan tells him so at the turn of the afternoon, in a voice scraped thin. The light in the shaft has crept back from nothing to a faint pearl haze, and in the old man's cupped palms the seed has swelled to the size of a plum. It pulses. It is warm. The small voice that comes from it is no longer a thread but a murmur, and it sounds, Jian thinks, a little more like the girl he first met.

I'm better, says Mei. Not good. But better. I had a very long sleep, and Papa told me stories, and I dreamed about a tree.

"What kind of tree?"

A big one with silver leaves. She sounds amused. I'm not sure it was nice to dream. But it wasn't frightening.

Jian does not answer at once. He is sitting on the cushions with his back against the wall of the platform, his staff across his knees, and he watches the light turn slowly in the old man's hands.

"Mei," he says, "I want to ask you something, and you need not answer."

You want to know if I'll do the next one.

"Yes."

Duan Ke. A small pause. He's the sword boy. The one who looks like he'd rather fight than sleep. She laughs, a little. I looked at him a long time while I was resting. He has a kind face. I think he's angry because he's afraid. But I'd like to meet him.

"It will cost you."

Seventeen percent. Papa did the sum. She says it cheerfully. That leaves forty-one. It's enough to keep the Gate going, if the lamps hold. And the lamps are holding.

"If it goes wrong—"

It won't. A firm little voice. And if it does, I'd rather it went wrong while I was helping.

Jian closes his eyes. Behind them the boy in his chest is silent, and warm, and very still.

She is brave, says the boy.

Yes.

Braver than me.

No, says Jian. Not braver. Only older.

* * *

They wake Duan Ke at dusk.

There is no ceremony. The children have been told, and have crowded into the Annex, and Nurse has set them in a row on the first cot with their feet dangling: Ao and Tao with the rabbit between them, Mo Yan with her charcoal, Zhen Li with the lamp, and Hai Ren, who has been allowed up for the first time, sitting a little apart with his long hands folded. He is pale. He is thin. He is entirely calm. When Jian looks at him, he inclines his head.

The sixth cot glows.

Duan Ke sleeps with the sword on his chest. It is a plain iron blade in a scabbard of black lacquer, no longer than his forearm, and his hands are clasped over the hilt. He is tall for sixteen, long in the arm, with a hard square jaw and a nose that has been broken once and set badly. His hair is bound in a topknot. His tunic is the coarse blue of an outer-court disciple. He looks, Jian thinks, like a boy who has spent too many nights dreaming of a duel.

The white ring turns. The hum rises in the floor. Mei's voice, soft and faint, says Seventeen, and then nothing.

And Duan Ke's eyes snap open.

He moves like a trap. One breath he is lying still; the next he is on his feet in the middle of the Annex, sword drawn, blade level, the black scabbard clattering on the floor. His back is to the wall. His eyes are wide and fixed. He has taken in the room in one sweep, the cots, the lamps, the faces, and his weight is forward on the balls of his feet, ready.

"Who is it?" he says. His voice is cracked and hard. "Who's there? Show yourself!"

Nobody moves. Ao has gone rigid on the cot. Tao's mouth is open. Jian lifts one hand, slowly, palm outward, and speaks in the calm voice he has used a thousand times on frightened recruits.

"Duan Ke. No one here means you harm."

The blade swings to him.

It is a beautiful stroke, steady, centered on his throat. The boy's wrist does not shake. He is looking at Jian's lined face, at the white-streaked hair and the staff and the pale gown, and the sword does not waver.

"You're old," he says, flatly.

"Yes."

"I don't know you."

"No. But you know the sword you hold. It is yours. It has been with you for a long time." Jian speaks slowly. "And you know that you are in a safe place. If you look around you, you will see that there are children."

Duan Ke's gaze flicks sideways. It takes in the cots, the small ones, the round-faced girl with her fist full of charcoal. The point of the blade dips, a fraction. He swallows.

"Where's the master?" he says. "Where's Master Ji?"

"He is gone," says Jian gently. "A very long time."

The sword lowers another inch.

* * *

It takes an hour to calm him.

Not because he is difficult. Because he is polite. He sheathes the blade when Nurse asks him, and bows to her, and apologizes. He sits when told. He drinks the tea she brings with both hands, and thanks her again. But his eyes keep going to the door, and the window, and the dark lamps, and his hands keep finding the hilt.

Bell sits with him, as she has sat with all the others, and tells him gently what has happened. She does not soften it. She says that he has slept for six hundred years. She says that the master he is asking for died long ago, along with the Sect, and the mountain, and the whole world that he knew. She says that he is one of seven, and that the others are in the room, and that they love him.

Duan Ke listens to it with his jaw set.

When she has finished, he says, "And the Sect?"

"Gone."

"The Heaven-Cleaving Sword Hall?"

"Gone. Long ago."

"Then who's fighting?" The question comes out raw. "Somebody has to be fighting. The beasts come every spring. The Wall needs men. If the Sect is gone, who holds it?"

Bell glances at Jian. He moves forward and sits down on the cot beside the boy.

"I do not know," he says. "That is the truth. There is a Wall, still. A different one. It holds a valley, and the people in it are my family and my friends. But the beasts you speak of are coming here first. We think in thirty days."

Duan Ke turns to look at him.

It is a long, searching look. The hard young face is thinner than it ought to be, and in the lamplight there are shadows under the eyes. But the eyes themselves are clear and dark and, Jian realizes, entirely sane.

"Then I'm needed," says Duan Ke.

"You are a guest."

"I am a disciple." He gets to his feet. He draws the sword and holds it flat across his palms, looking at the dull iron. "I was trained for exactly this. I was not made to sleep for six hundred years. I was made to hold a wall." He sheathes it with a click. "Show me where the enemy comes from, old man, and I will stand there."

* * *

They show him in the end because he will not be put off.

He stands at the head of the spiral stair on the ninth terrace, where the lamps are dark and the blue light of the sleeping beds shows faintly through the gloom. Jian stands behind him with Bell, and Yue at the rail with her hand on the floor, and Zhen Li, white-faced, with his lamp. Behind them, in the corridor, the others have been told to stay.

The dark is very thick down here.

It is not a natural dark. It lies on the terrace like a weight. Jian can feel it on his skin, cold and faintly greasy, and he knows from the way Yue stiffens that she is feeling it too, in the floor. The air smells of wet stone and old blood. At the far end of the terrace, perhaps eighty paces away, a ring of broken lamps hangs over a round grated drain in the floor.

"There," says Zhen Li. "That's where it went."

Duan Ke is silent. He crosses to the rail and looks down at the grate. Then he turns to Jian and says, "How many lamps would it take to seal that?"

"I do not know."

"How many has your boy lit?"

"A hundred and nineteen."

"And how many are dark?"

"A hundred and ninety."

"Not enough." The sword boy folds his arms. "A seal must hold. If the beasts come for the dark, they will come where it is thickest. They will come here. Not in thirty days. Tonight."

Jian's stomach turns. "Tonight?"

"If I were a scout, and I had come to look, and a boy with a lamp had chased me down a drain, I would go back and tell my captain exactly where the weak door was." Duan Ke's mouth is grim. "I would tell him to bring friends."

Beside Jian, Yue goes rigid. She seizes his sleeve and presses her palm flat against the boards, and her face goes the color of paper.

She writes one word on the slate, in letters so large that the chalk breaks.

Now.

* * *

Between the terrace and the fall of night, Jian does something he has not done in decades: he makes a plan.

He draws it on the slate with a stub of chalk, sitting on the end of the eighth cot with the children gathered round. It is a simple thing. A ring for the Annex, a line for the corridor, an X for the ninth terrace, and a scatter of small dots where Zhen Li's lamps burn. Duan Ke leans over his shoulder with his arms crossed, and every few seconds he reaches out and moves a mark with one blistered finger.

"Not there. If it comes up on this side, it has the stair behind it." He taps the line. "You want it at the grate. A drain is a throat. Let it come through one at a time, and cut it as it climbs."

"And the others?"

"Back. Behind the first lamp. A beast that hates the light will not cross a lit threshold unless it is mad with hunger." He glances sidelong. "Tell the little ones to stay. If they see it, they will scream, and screaming draws it."

"Yue can feel it through the floor," says Jian. "She will signal."

"Good." The sword boy nods slowly. "How does she signal?"

Yue, who has been reading his lips with her chin in her fist, holds up the slate. Stamp three times. Below it she has drawn a small foot.

Duan Ke looks at the drawing. His mouth twitches, once.

"You," he says, "are going to be very useful."

She ducks her head. For a moment she looks, Jian thinks, like the shy girl who first came to the valley with a pebble round her neck and a silence she did not yet know how to fill.

* * *

Hai Ren finds Duan Ke on the terrace stair, an hour before midnight.

Jian happens upon them by chance, leaning on the staff at the turn of the corridor, and he stops in the shadow because neither of them has noticed him. The sword boy sits on the top step with his cracked blade across his knees, rubbing the lacquer of the sheath with a rag. The monk stands two steps below, tall and thin in his gray robe, hands folded, with the stillness of a candle in a windless room.

"You will fight," says Hai Ren.

"I will."

"It will cost you."

"Everything costs." Duan Ke does not look up. "You think I don't know? You were the one who walked the terraces and put the dying to rest. I saw the way you shook. I'd call that a cost."

"It was." The quiet voice is without offense. "I did not mean to rebuke you. I only wished to say that I understand."

"Understand what?"

"That you are afraid."

Duan Ke's hands stop on the rag. For a long moment there is no sound but the faint tick of a lamp cooling somewhere below. Then, roughly, he says, "I'm not."

"I think you are. I think you were afraid before you slept, and you were afraid when you woke, and you have been afraid for six hundred years. It is the fear that makes you good." Hai Ren inclines his head. "I only want you to know that it is permitted to be afraid and to fight. The Quiet School taught that stillness is for those who do not fear. But I have lately come to think that the greater stillness is the stillness of those who do."

Duan Ke's jaw works. He looks at the monk. And then, slowly, as if the muscles were unwilling, he puts out a hand.

Hai Ren takes it. They stay like that for a time, the swordsman and the monk, two boys in the lamp-lit dark, holding hands on a stair.

Jian slips away without a sound.

* * *

The grate bursts at midnight.

There is no warning. One moment the dark terrace is still; the next, with a shriek of iron, the round grating at the end of the floor tears upward and flies across the room, striking the far wall with a crash that shakes dust from the vault. Something pours up out of the hole. It is pale, and wet, and many-legged, and it moves in a rush of clicking sound like a spilled box of knives.

A crawler.

Jian has seen their kind before. On the road, in the Ash Marches, in the dead cities under the mountain. They are long, low things, the size of an ox, with six jointed legs and a flat blind head crowned with a ring of bone. This one is larger than any he has seen. The head scrapes the ceiling. The legs, tipped with hooked spurs, cut grooves in the stone as it scuttles forward. Its hide is the color of a drowned man's skin, and where the lamplight touches it, it hisses.

Bell screams something. Yue is dragging Zhen Li back. The boy's lamp has dimmed to a spark in his fist.

And Duan Ke walks forward.

He does not run. He does not shout. He steps out of the line of the stair onto the open floor of the terrace, and he draws the blade from its black lacquer scabbard in a single smooth pull, and he drops into a low stance with the point toward the thing's eyes. His feet are bare. His topknot has come loose. He looks, Jian thinks, impossibly young.

The crawler lunges.

It is very fast. A pale streak of legs and hooks, and the boy is in the way of it, and Jian's voice rises in a cry. But Duan Ke is not there when the legs close. He has dropped, rolled, turned. The iron blade flashes once in the amber lamplight, a single clean arc, and the crawler's foremost leg falls to the floor, severed at the joint.

It screams. It is a horrible sound, high and thin. It whirls, and the ring of bone on its head swings like a club.

The boy ducks under it.

He is quick. Jian has watched Han drill his guards and Lan Wen spar with the juniors, and he has never seen a boy move like this. There is no waste in him. Each step is a measure, each cut a sentence. The sword flickers in the dimness, turning aside hooks, slicing at joints, pivoting always toward the soft place behind the bone ring. A second leg falls. A third. The crawler staggers, its hide split along three long wounds, oozing a clear greenish fluid that sizzles on the floor.

"Fall back," Duan Ke calls, without turning. "The lamp! Bring me the light!"

Zhen Li staggers forward. He has the brass lamp in both fists, and he thrusts it into the air above his head, and the little flame blazes up, white and gold, filling the terrace with a hot clear radiance. The crawler shrieks again and flinches. The blind head swings, uncertain.

Duan Ke leaps.

He goes up its back like a monkey. One foot on the stump of a leg, the other on the hump of the shoulder, the sword raised overhead in both hands. For one frozen instant he hangs in the lamplight, a slim dark figure against the pale bulk of the beast.

Then he brings the blade down.

It goes through the bone ring and into the skull beneath with a crunch that Jian feels in his own teeth. The crawler convulses. The legs fold. It collapses, in a long shuddering slide, to the stone floor, and the boy rides it down with the sword still buried to the hilt, and the green fluid spurts up in a fountain and soaks him to the knees.

Silence.

Then, from the far end of the terrace, a thin high sound: a child's cheer.

* * *

It is Tao.

Jian never learns how the boy got past the corridor. He is standing at the head of the stair in his nightgown, with his top in his fist and his face blazing, jumping up and down on the spot and shouting something that is lost in the echoes. Behind him, Ao is dancing. Mo Yan has drawn a picture on the wall. Hai Ren stands among them, with his hands folded, looking at the dead beast with grave attention, and Nurse is crying openly into her apron.

Bell reaches Duan Ke first. He is on his knees by the corpse with his hands on the hilt of his sword, shaking. She drops down beside him and seizes his wrists.

"Are you hurt?"

"No." He looks at his hands. "I think it burned a little."

It has. The skin of his forearms is red and blistered where the green fluid soaked through his sleeves, a fine peppering of small burns. Bell hisses between her teeth and calls for water, and Yue is already there with a flask. Duan Ke endures it with perfect stoicism. When she has bound him up, he draws the sword free of the carcass and holds it up to the lamp.

The blade is cracked.

A long hairline fracture runs from the point to the guard. It will not hold another blow. He stares at it, and his face does something complicated, and then he lays the sword gently across his knees.

"It was my father's," he says.

"I'm sorry," says Jian.

"Don't be." The boy lifts his chin. His eyes are bright and fierce and wet. "It did what it was made for. I'd rather it broke on something worth the breaking."

Nurse comes up the stair then, with a long cloth bundle in her arms.

Her face is composed. She has stopped crying. She kneels in her apron beside the boy and sets the bundle down next to the cracked blade, and unwraps the cloth with careful, deliberate fingers.

It is a sword.

Not iron. The blade is a long narrow leaf of pale metal, bright as a mirror, with a faint blue shimmer in the edge. The hilt is wrapped in worn black cord. The guard is a plain bar. It weighs, when Duan Ke takes it in both hands, almost nothing at all.

"What is it?" he whispers.

"It was Operator Five's," says Nurse. "Mr. Cole's. He had it made in the first year. He said that if one of the children ever woke wanting to fight, he would like them to have something better than what they came with." Her voice is low. "I have kept it oiled for six hundred years. I did not think I would ever give it away."

Duan Ke stares at the bright blade. "I can't—"

"You can." She folds his fingers round the hilt. "It was made for you. I only held it."

He is silent a long time. Then he bows his head over the sword, very deep, until his forehead nearly touches the blade, and Nurse lays her small round hand on the back of his neck.

"Thank you," says Duan Ke.

"Don't thank me," says Nurse. "Break it on something worth the breaking."

Jian looks at the sword, and the boy, and the dead thing sprawled across the stone, and the small figures cheering at the head of the stair. He thinks of Han on the Wall, and of the long white road, and of sixty days. He feels, for the first time since the Gate, something he had almost forgotten.

Hope.

From the stair, Tao's voice rises once more, high and fierce and entirely unselfconscious. "Do it again!" he shrieks. "Do it again, Duan Ke! Do the one with the flip!"

The sword boy turns his head. For the first time since he woke, he is almost smiling. It is a stiff, embarrassed, reluctant thing, as though the muscles have forgotten the shape, but it is a smile all the same.

"Not tonight," he calls back.

"Tomorrow?"

"Tomorrow, maybe."

Tao whoops. Ao claps. Even Mo Yan, on the stair, is hopping on one foot. And Jian, leaning on his staff in the lamplight with a dead beast at his feet, finds that he is smiling too.

```
STANDBY :: Hostile eliminated. Classification: Seam-crawler (juvenile).
THREAT FORECAST :: Next incursion in 6–9 days. Scale: 3–5 units.
NOTE: Operator 3 (Duan Ke): swordsmanship verified. Value: high.
```

"Six days," Jian says aloud.

Duan Ke looks up.

"Teach me," says the boy. "Tell me how many, and from where, and I will teach the rest of you how to hold."
